# Open-source software for clinical trial recruitment

MatchMiner is a suite of tools that helps cancer centers find eligible patients and fill their trials, from the trial office to the medical record. It has been built and used at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute since 2016.

::: {.hero-actions}
[Explore the tools](#suite){.btn .btn-warning}
[Code and models](open-source.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-light}
:::
:::

::: {.intro-copy}
## Why trial matching is hard

Clinical trials are how new cancer treatments reach patients. Yet fewer than 1 in 10 adults with cancer take part,<sup class="cite"><a href="#src-unger">1</a></sup> and many trials miss their enrollment goals or never finish.<sup class="cite"><a href="#src-cheng">2</a>,<a href="#src-stensland">3</a></sup>

Oncology trials are complex, with multiple arms and narrowly defined eligibility, often including specific treatment and biomarker requirements.<sup class="cite"><a href="#src-jin">4</a></sup> Working through those criteria for every patient takes time that oncologists and trial teams rarely have. MatchMiner does that work at scale, checking patients against every open trial so oncologists and trial teams see the trials each patient may qualify for.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="gap-stats">
  <dl>
    <div>
      <dt>8%</dt>
      <dd>of patients with cancer enroll in a clinical trial<sup class="cite"><a href="#src-unger">1</a></sup></dd>
    </div>
    <div>
      <dt>37%</dt>
      <dd>of NCI-sponsored cancer trials in one analysis missed their minimum enrollment goal<sup class="cite"><a href="#src-cheng">2</a></sup></dd>
    </div>
  </dl>
</div>
```

:::

::: {.pillars}

::: {.pillar}
[Genomic matching]{.pillar-kind}

### MatchMiner Genomics

[Patients with the specific genomic alterations a trial needs are hard to find by hand.]{.pillar-problem}

Each trial's eligibility is written in a structured format, and a matching engine checks every patient's sequencing results against it. It finds trials for a patient and patients for a trial.

[In clinical use at Dana-Farber since 2016.]{.pillar-status}

[About Genomics](genomics.qmd)
:::

::: {.pillar}
[AI matching]{.pillar-kind}

### MatchMiner-AI

[Details that decide eligibility, like prior treatment, are often found only in clinical notes.]{.pillar-problem}

Language models read a patient's clinical notes and match them against all open trials, not only genomically driven ones. Oncologists review the suggested trials, each with a plain-language summary.

[Launched for Dana-Farber providers in February 2026.]{.pillar-status}

[About MatchMiner-AI](matchminer-ai.qmd)
:::

::: {.pillar}
[Trial operations]{.pillar-kind}

### MatchMiner Dashboard

[Trial teams track open trials, slots, and accrual across several systems and a lot of email.]{.pillar-problem}

One view of the trials a disease-specific trial team runs: open slots, enrollment, and milestones. Details come from ClinicalTrials.gov and the center's clinical trial management system (CTMS), and teams add eligibility notes.

[In production at Dana-Farber across several disease-specific trial teams.]{.pillar-status}

[About Dashboard](dashboard.qmd)
:::

## Open code, open models

The matching engine, the web application, and MatchMiner-AI's model weights, inference code, and synthetic training data are all public. Any cancer center can run them inside its own network and see exactly how a match was made. The Dashboard code is due for release in winter 2026–27.

Other centers already build on it. Princess Margaret Cancer Centre in Toronto leads CTIMS, an open-source trial matching system that uses the MatchMiner matching engine. [See who uses MatchMiner.](adopters.qmd)
:::

## In daily use, tested in trials

MatchMiner has run at Dana-Farber since 2016. Providers now open it from the patient's record in Epic, Dana-Farber's electronic health record.

Dana-Farber also runs randomized studies to learn how best to get matches in front of oncologists, and changes the design based on the results.
:::

::: {.evidence-list}

::: {.evidence-item}
[Randomized trial, 2023–2024]{.evidence-when}

When AI detected that a patient's cancer was progressing, their oncologist got an email about genomic trial matches from MatchMiner. The AI reliably spotted patients likely to need a new treatment, but the emails alone didn't raise enrollment.

[Results in JAMA Network Open, 2025](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2833029)
:::

::: {.evidence-item}
[Randomized trial, recruiting since 2026]{.evidence-when}

OPTIONS-ACTIVATE sends oncologists a ranked list of trials from MatchMiner-AI when progression is detected, and measures the share of new treatments that are clinical trials.

[About OPTIONS-ACTIVATE](news/posts/2026-options-activate.qmd)
:::
